channel.title: Dragonfly Lens - new research
channel.description: Plain-English, source-led research on the physical AI build-out. Independent; every figure dated and sourced; corrections logged, never deleted.

item.title: Is Your Backtest Lying To You?
item.description: Nine ways our own backtests lied, nine checks that would have caught most of them, what those checks still miss, and how the ideas did once the tests were fixed.

item.title: Before the Screens: Who Got Paid on the Trading Floor
item.description: Nasdaq plans a 9 pm to 4 am session from 6 December. We traced where trading-floor money came from and what screens changed, then tested whether round-the-clock venues shrink market gaps. Two of our guesses failed, and so did one of our own results.

item.title: Why Canada's Budget Numbers Do Not Match
item.description: Posts say Ottawa will borrow $733 billion to cover $333 billion of deficits. We reconciled the PBO's own tables, compared Canada with other countries' debt histories, priced a 10, 15 and 20 year path to a balanced budget, and sized the documented waste and fraud against the deficit.

item.title: Data Centres Use Water. So Does Your Lawn. Compared to What?
item.description: A popular claim says golf courses use about three times the water of data centres. The primary reports measure different things, so they cannot settle it, and a national total cannot settle where water is a problem.

item.title: A Viral Post Says Plasma Can Turn CO2 Into Fuel. Here Is What the Yale Paper Says.
item.description: A viral post says Yale scientists turned carbon dioxide into fuel with plasma, powered by solar. We checked it against the paper's abstract and supplement and Yale's release. The chemistry is real; the practical claims have not been shown beyond the lab.

item.title: Did Canada Send Ukraine $30 Billion? What the Government's Own Numbers Say
item.description: The viral $30 billion claim is too high. Canada's own figure is over $25.5 billion. Where the money went, who checked it, the refinery comparison, what cutting aid would free up, and what is not yet public about repayment.

item.title: The Vertical Farm Was Never The Answer. The Boiler Is.
item.description: A 2025 industry compilation counted fourteen indoor-farming bankruptcies and closures worldwide. The question was never whether to grow food indoors - it is what, and next to what. Canadian yields, the heat problem, and what a cold city of 250,000 would actually need.

item.title: Growth Is 3.4% Of The Openings
item.description: Every fastest-growing-careers list ranks the smallest part of the number. Across the US economy, genuinely new jobs are 3.4% of annual openings. The other 96.6% is people leaving.

item.title: The AI Build-Out Makes Two Things Nobody Is Bidding For
item.description: Data centres produce waste heat continuously and retired hardware on a schedule set by depreciation policy. One has a price in exactly one city. The other just showed up in Amazon's accounts.

item.title: Our Data Was Lying for Five Months. Every Alarm Said It Was Fine.
item.description: One of our internal trading research projects never worked. The edge was manufactured by a defect in our own price data - two versions of history mixed together, bar by bar, inside the same trading day. Every integrity check we had passed it, because every single price in the file was real. Here is how data lies while looking healthy, and the one test that catches it.

item.title: We Published the Wrong Number. Here Is the Right One.
item.description: A correction of our own track-record figures, and the three questions that let you check anyone's track record in two minutes. Every figure in it was withdrawn on 6 November 2026, when we found the underlying table's entry dates were chosen with hindsight.

item.title: We Found a Real Edge. It Died in 2017. That Was Predictable.
item.description: Huge pension funds are forced to sell stocks at the end of certain months. That is not a theory - it is a rule they cannot refuse. We found the pattern it leaves in prices, confirmed it across four US indices and a European market, and then watched it vanish after 2017. Why it died explains which market patterns survive becoming famous, and which never do.

item.title: The $7 Trillion Market That $280 Million Moved
item.description: In January, roughly $280 million of trading repriced Japan's $7.2 trillion government bond market. That is not a solvency story, it is a liquidity one - and the reason is that the buyer left. How banking actually works, why the interest rate matters more than the debt level, and what indebted countries can realistically do about it.

item.title: The Americas Trade: What the Hemisphere Strategy Bets On
item.description: Washington has reasserted the Monroe Doctrine in writing. Strip out the noise and the strategy is a bet on the hemisphere's resources - oil, copper, lithium, uranium, food, water - and on keeping China out of them. Here is what the Americas actually hold, country by country, what each should lean into, and the honest test: which moves make sense now, which only on a 20-year clock, and which cannot be judged yet.

item.title: Geothermal Went Public. 12 Days Later, Its Well Blew Out.
item.description: Fervo Energy raised $1.9 billion in clean energy's biggest IPO, then suffered a well blowout at its flagship Utah project. Here is the honest promise-and-setback read on next-generation geothermal, the heat batteries quietly scaling beside it, and who gets paid if 24/7 heat from the ground becomes AI's firm power.

item.title: The Robot Decades: An Honest Timeline for the Machines
item.description: Everyone has a number for when robots take the jobs. Most are marketing. Here is the sober version: four scenarios for 2040, the rule that predicts which jobs go first, the profession that was declared dead in 2016 and got a raise instead - and the question that matters more than the timeline: who owns the robots.

item.title: AI's Next Bottleneck Is the Wire Between the Chips
item.description: AI chips have outrun the copper wires that connect them. The fix is to send data as light, right next to the chip - and that needs lasers built on a rare crystal (indium phosphide) that only a few firms make on tiny wafers. Lumentum's CEO calls the coming shortage 'worse than memory.' Plain English, every number sourced.

item.title: Big Tech Is Going Nuclear: What’s Real and Who Gets Paid
item.description: Microsoft, Amazon and Google are all buying nuclear power for AI. But the only near-term megawatts come from restarting old reactors; the shiny small-reactor and fusion headlines are 2030s-and-later targets — and the fuel they need is enriched by Russia and China. Plain English, every date sourced, hype flagged.

item.title: The Musk Playbook: Own the Bottleneck, Don't Rent It
item.description: Look past the personality and Elon Musk's companies rhyme: each one seizes a different bottleneck in the AI and energy buildout, and they feed each other. Tesla makes the power, xAI makes the intelligence, the new $16.8B Terafab makes the chips, SpaceX makes the launch and the connectivity. The lesson isn't 'buy Tesla' - it's where the value pools. Plain English, every number sourced, hype flagged.

item.title: GameStop Wasn't Magic. It Was a Setup You Can Learn to Read.
item.description: In 2021 a struggling game retailer went from $17 to $483 and cost hedge funds about $5 billion. It looked like chaos - it wasn't. The setup was sitting in public data anyone could read. Here's how a short squeeze actually works, how to spot the setup yourself, and the part nobody tells you: most people who chased it late got wrecked. Plain English, every number sourced.

item.title: Why Dragonfly Lens Exists - Read This First
item.description: Before you read anything else here, read this. Who we are, what we're trying to do, and the promise we make you: plain-English research on the markets that matter, every claim sourced, hype flagged, and a public log of when we're wrong. Built for regular people, by an independent, self-funded team - not Wall Street.

item.title: AI’s Real Bottleneck Isn’t the Chip. It’s the Memory Wall
item.description: In one week of August 2026, Anthropic started designing its own chips and AMD bought a startup that bakes AI models straight into silicon. Different headlines, same story: the bottleneck has moved from the processor to the memory feeding it — the 'memory wall.' Whoever wins, the memory makers and the one factory underneath them get paid. Plain English, every number sourced.

item.title: Nobody Knows the Price: Valuing Under Uncertainty
item.description: A backtest glowed with a Sharpe ratio of 40. We deleted it on purpose. What Mises, Knight, Hayek, Mandelbrot, Taleb, Keynes, Soros, and even the efficient-market crowd teach about why markets humble the confident - and why the real edge is discipline, not a secret formula.

item.title: The Synchronization Problem: Gigawatts Aren’t Compute
item.description: The AI build-out is quoted in announcements - '10 GW', '$750B capex' - but almost none of it is compute yet. Every input arrives on a different clock, and the slowest one sets the date. A plain-English look at the critical path, the synchronization tax, and a scorecard for reading any data-center headline.

item.title: The Data Center That Feeds You: A Practical Blueprint
item.description: AI data centers dump gigawatts of low-grade heat into the sky while greenhouses next door burn gas to stay warm. A practical, numbers-first design for pairing them - the loop, the crops, the economics, the risks - and why regulators just made it inevitable.

item.title: The AI Goes Public: What to Read When the S-1 Drops
item.description: Anthropic and OpenAI filed to IPO. Before you buy the hype, here's the calm, numbers-first checklist for the public S-1: the real losses, the compute liabilities, gross margin, lock-ups - plus whether you should even buy an IPO at all.

item.title: Kurzweil's Compass, Not His Calendar
item.description: The '42% right' takedown of Ray Kurzweil measures the wrong thing. Judge a futurist on direction, sequence, and magnitude - not exact dates - and his record is remarkable. The honest, plain-English case, and what it means for your money.

item.title: Dividends 101 - Getting Paid to Own Stocks (Plain English)
item.description: What a dividend actually is, what yield really means (and why a high one is often a warning), the one date that matters (ex-dividend), reinvesting and the snowball, growth vs high yield, and the tax angle - all in plain English, with a quiz.

item.title: The Agent Economy: Why AI Will Pay On-Chain - Plain English
item.description: The next wave of software is AI agents that act on your behalf - and they need to pay for things instantly, in tiny amounts, around the clock. Our card and bank rails can't do that. Here's why blockchains and stablecoins might be the real engine of crypto. Plain English, with a quiz.

item.title: What Blockchain Actually Is - No Hype, Plain English
item.description: Forget the price charts and the hype. Here's what a blockchain actually is, why money was never magic in the first place, why it could be the future of money - and why most crypto is still junk. Plain English, with a quiz at the end.

item.title: The Dotcom Playbook for Crypto - Telling Real From Junk
item.description: In 1999 hundreds of internet companies went public on hype. Most went to zero - a few became giants. Crypto is the same shape. Here's the plain-English checklist for telling the rare real projects from the ~95% that will be worth nothing, plus a quiz.

item.title: Money Has Always Been Trust: A 5-Minute History
item.description: From seashells to the dollar to crypto, money has always been one thing: whatever a society agrees to trust. A short, plain-English history that explains why 'backed by nothing' is true of the dollar too - plus a quiz at the end.

item.title: Start Early: Why Time Is Your Biggest Edge
item.description: The biggest secret in investing isn't a hot stock - it's time. Move the sliders and watch a small monthly habit become a retirement. Plain English, with the real accounts that make it happen.

item.title: Tokenization: When Everything Becomes Tradeable
item.description: Tokenization turns real assets - stocks, bonds, gold, buildings, funds - into digital tokens you can own and trade instantly, 24/7, in tiny fractions. Here's what's real (BlackRock, Franklin Templeton, tokenized treasuries), what's hype, and the risks. Plain English, with a quiz.

item.title: Nvidia's Biggest Threat Is Its Own Customers
item.description: Amazon and Google — two of Nvidia's biggest customers — are now building and selling their own AI chips. That sounds like Nvidia's problem. But the company that designs those custom chips, and the single factory that makes every chip in the story, get paid no matter who wins. Bet the bottleneck, not the horse. Plain English, every number sourced.

item.title: The CPU Comeback: Why AI Agents Put the CPU Back in Charge
item.description: Everyone wrote off the CPU when GPUs won the AI training war. Then AI became agents — and a huge share of the work turned out to be logic, not math. Here's why the 'boring' chip is the surprise winner of the agent era, what 'CPU comeback' really means (ARM, not x86), and who profits. Plain English, every number sourced.

item.title: How to Read a Dividend Without Getting Trapped
item.description: A 12% yield looks like free money. It's usually a warning. The highest dividend yields are almost always the market screaming that a cut is coming. Here's how to tell a dividend you can trust from a trap — the four checks (and the one filter that does the most work). Plain English.

item.title: The Next Bottleneck Isn't Silicon. It's Light.
item.description: For 50 years, AI's limit was 'more transistors.' That era is ending. The real wall now is moving data between chips — and the energy it burns. The fix is light. Here's why co-packaged optics is the most important hardware shift of the decade, who profits, and an honest moonshot ladder. Plain English, every claim sourced.

item.title: The Miners Quietly Becoming AI Landlords
item.description: A bitcoin miner just signed a $220M deal to run AI for Bell Canada and Cohere. It's the clearest sign yet of a quiet rotation: crypto miners with cheap power and ready data centers are turning into AI compute landlords — while the market still prices some like hash machines. Who's really pivoting, who's just saying it, and the honest risks. Plain English, every number sourced.

item.title: AI Is Reopening Dead Nuclear Plants
item.description: A nuclear reactor that shut down in 2019 is being brought back to life — specifically to power AI data centers. Canada just finished a major reactor refurb seven months early and under budget. The 'nuclear is dead' consensus is reversing in real time, and AI's bottomless power demand is the reason. Who profits, plain English, every number sourced.
